strengths: The paper investigates an important question: whether SAM's generalization improvements come with increased membership leakage. Connecting optimization, atypical examples, and privacy is a worthwhile contribution.
The influence-based grouping provides an informative descriptive analysis of where SAM and SWA improve accuracy. The accompanying image examples help interpret the groups.
Experiments cover four image and tabular datasets, multiple attack types, and additional image architectures. Higher single-query attack accuracy for SAM recurs across the tested image architectures.

SharpReg is a simple optimization modification with promising empirical tradeoffs. On CIFAR-100, reported single-query attack accuracy decreases from 76.68% to 59.64%, while test accuracy decreases from 79.92% to 75.86%.
weaknesses: The central influence-entropy metric is not mathematically well specified. Influence scores can be negative, so normalization in Equation (3) need not produce probabilities. All-zero scores produce 0/0, yet Appendix C.1 assigns 2,153 such test examples to the highest-entropy bucket. The transformation, zero handling, and sensitivity to these choices require explicit justification.

The experiments do not directly establish that SAM memorizes more. Buckets are constructed from precomputed SGD influence scores; better SAM accuracy within these buckets can also reflect better representation learning. SAM-specific counterfactual influence measurements are missing, and near-ceiling accuracy in the highest bucket complicates comparisons of absolute gains. The mechanistic analysis is also confined to CIFAR-100.

The privacy conclusions need qualification. SAM reduces label-only attack accuracy from 69.18% to 65.41% on CIFAR-100 and from 56.36% to 54.01% on CIFAR-10. Its single-query increase on Purchase-100 is only 0.29 percentage points, smaller than the reported standard deviations. These results support a narrower claim about the strongest evaluated attacks; the opposing attack trends remain unexplained. Calibrated likelihood-ratio attacks and true-positive rates at low false-positive rates are missing.

There is an apparent inconsistency in attack reporting. Table 3 gives 77.04% correctness-based attack accuracy for CIFAR-100/SGD, whereas Equation (8) and Table 4's 99.98% training and 80.30% test accuracies imply approximately 59.84% under balanced membership evaluation. Exact attack-set sizes, membership balance, and table labels must be clarified to reconcile these results.

SharpReg's proposed anti-overfitting mechanism is insufficiently justified. For ξ<1, Equation (5) equals (1−ξ) times Equation (4) with λ replaced by λ/(1−ξ). Although Appendix C.4.1 acknowledges parameter redundancy, ξ does not introduce an independent regularizer. Controls for effective sharpness strength, loss scaling, and learning rate are needed to support its interpretation as an early-stopping proxy.

The mitigation comparison does not establish an advantage over appropriately tuned conventional regularization. Matched-accuracy comparisons with early-stopped SGD and weight-decay or dropout sweeps are missing. SELENA outperforms the default SharpReg setting on both utility and both attack accuracies for CIFAR-100 and Texas-100 in Table 4. Computational simplicity is appealing, but runtime measurements are absent. These unresolved methodological and evaluation issues place the submission below the acceptance threshold.
